event_overview.title: About Gaza Conflict
event_overview.subject: Gaza Conflict
event_overview.summary: The Gaza conflict refers here to the war that began after Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups attacked southern Israel on 7 October 2023, killing people and taking hostages, followed by Israel's large-scale military campaign in the Gaza Strip. The conflict has involved air, ground and naval operations, rocket fire, hostage issues, severe civilian harm and displacement, humanitarian-access disputes, and international legal and diplomatic action.

facts.label: Start and status
facts.value: The current war began on 7 October 2023. Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups attacked Israel from Gaza; Israel then declared war and began military operations in Gaza. The conflict remained active during the period covered by the selected timeline.

facts.label: Main parties and setting
facts.value: The principal military parties are Israel and Hamas, alongside other Palestinian armed groups. The main theatre is the Gaza Strip, a densely populated Palestinian territory bordering Israel and Egypt; attacks and consequences have also affected Israel and the wider occupied Palestinian territory.

facts.label: Hostages
facts.value: Hamas and other armed groups abducted 251 people during the 7 October attack, making the release, recovery and treatment of hostages a central issue in ceasefire and negotiation efforts.

facts.label: Humanitarian effects
facts.value: United Nations reporting describes extensive damage to civilian infrastructure, repeated mass displacement and major constraints on humanitarian assistance in Gaza. Health facilities, water and sanitation systems, shelters, roads and aid operations have all been affected by the hostilities and access restrictions.

facts.label: International legal context
facts.value: The International Court of Justice is hearing South Africa's case against Israel under the Genocide Convention. In 2024, the Court issued provisional measures, including measures relating to Rafah and humanitarian access; such measures are interim orders and do not constitute a final ruling on the merits of the allegations.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows particular reported developments in Gaza during August and September 2026, especially strikes, casualties, medical and camp conditions, diplomacy and investigations; it does not provide a complete record of the war, negotiations, humanitarian situation or events elsewhere.

sections.heading: Demographic Forces Behind Muslim Growth
sections.body: Pew estimates that Muslim women had an average total fertility rate of 3.1 children from 2020 to 2025, compared with 2.5 among Christian women. Its Muslim population is projected to grow from 369 million to 980 million, increasing the region’s share of Muslims worldwide from 18% to 27%.

sections.heading: Christianity Remains Regionally Predominant

explore_lenses.label: How will Senate Democrats choose their leader?
explore_lenses.title: A private, majority-ballot election
explore_lenses.summary: This is an internal Democratic Conference election, not a vote of the full Senate. The caucus rules require a secret ballot and repeated rounds if necessary until a candidate wins a majority of members present and voting.

claims.text: The Democratic Conference rules require contested leadership elections to be conducted by secret ballot and in person; proxies are permitted.
If neither candidate wins a majority on the first ballot, the rules require successive ballots without interruption or recess until a candidate has a majority of members present and voting.

The Conference, rather than the full Senate, selects and confirms its officers; its rules allow these elections beginning in December before a new Congress. Associated Press reported that this contest is expected in early December.

story_report.summary: Chuck Schumer, the Senate’s incumbent Democratic minority leader, is facing a leadership challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen as Democrats prepare to lead the chamber. The contest has exposed competing views of what the party’s electoral success means and whether its next leader should preserve or change its direction. Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton has dismissed the fight as a “performance,” while the confidential vote leaves the outcome unsettled.

sections.heading: Van Hollen’s Case for Change
sections.body: Van Hollen says he entered the race because voters demanded change from both Trump’s policies and a status quo he says is failing working people, arguing that the moment requires new leadership. Sen. Bernie Sanders, who supports Van Hollen, frames the choice as whether Democrats become more rooted in grassroots and working-family politics while confronting concentrated wealth and special interests. Sen. Jeff Merkley likewise endorsed Van Hollen, saying government should serve people rather than privileged and powerful interests.

sections.heading: Schumer Cites Democratic Midterm Gains
sections.body: Schumer says Democrats won 55 seats and counting, believes he has the votes to remain leader, and wants to lead the incoming majority in delivering for the public. Sen. Angus King, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, backed Schumer, citing his role in the election result, his proposed voter-responsive agenda and his command of Senate procedure. Reporting says Schumer recruited and raised money for winning candidates, while critics contend the electoral wave was driven chiefly by voters rather than Washington leadership.

sections.heading: Democratic Conference Vote Procedures
sections.body: The Democratic Conference—not the full Senate—selects and confirms its officers. Under conference rules, a contested leadership election must be conducted in person by secret ballot, although proxies are permitted; if no candidate wins an initial majority, ballots continue without interruption or recess until a candidate secures a majority of members present and voting. The rules permit such elections to begin in December before a new Congress, and the contest has been reported as expected in early December.

event_overview.title: About Iran War
event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: The Iran War is an ongoing armed conflict centered on military operations by the United States and Israel against Iran, Iranian retaliation, and a parallel struggle over security and commercial navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. The conflict has also affected neighboring Gulf states, international shipping, energy markets, and diplomatic efforts to establish a ceasefire or longer-term settlement.

facts.label: Start and status
facts.value: U.S. and Israeli military operations against Iran began on February 28, 2026; major combat was paused by an April 7 U.S.-Iran ceasefire, but hostilities and attacks affecting shipping resumed in July 2026.

facts.label: Central geography
facts.value: The Strait of Hormuz is a principal focus of the conflict. It links the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman, lies within Iranian and Omani territorial waters, and is a major route for oil and liquefied-natural-gas trade.

facts.label: Main participants and spillover
facts.value: The core interstate conflict involves Iran and the United States, with Israel participating alongside the United States; attacks and threats have also affected commercial vessels and Gulf countries including Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

facts.label: Diplomatic framework
facts.value: On June 17, 2026, the United States and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding that envisaged ending military operations and Iranian arrangements for safe commercial passage through the Strait for 60 days; its interpretation and implementation became contested.

facts.label: International legal and humanitarian con
facts.value: United Nations Security Council documentation has emphasized that transit passage through the Strait should not be impeded, called for protection of civilian infrastructure and commercial shipping, and urged de-escalation and diplomacy.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers a short period of escalation and negotiation in late July 2026, especially threats, maritime-security incidents and U.S. domestic war-powers debate; it does not cover the conflict's full military, diplomatic, humanitarian or regional history.

event_overview.title: About Iran War
event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: The Iran War is an ongoing armed conflict centered on military operations by the United States and Israel against Iran, Iranian retaliation, and a parallel struggle over security and commercial navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. The conflict has also affected neighboring Gulf states, international shipping, energy markets, and diplomatic efforts to establish a ceasefire or longer-term settlement.

facts.label: Start and status
facts.value: U.S. and Israeli military operations against Iran began on February 28, 2026; major combat was paused by an April 7 U.S.-Iran ceasefire, but hostilities and attacks affecting shipping resumed in July 2026.

facts.label: Central geography
facts.value: The Strait of Hormuz is a principal focus of the conflict. It links the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman, lies within Iranian and Omani territorial waters, and is a major route for oil and liquefied-natural-gas trade.

facts.label: Main participants and spillover
facts.value: The core interstate conflict involves Iran and the United States, with Israel participating alongside the United States; attacks and threats have also affected commercial vessels and Gulf countries including Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

facts.label: Diplomatic framework
facts.value: On June 17, 2026, the United States and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding that envisaged ending military operations and Iranian arrangements for safe commercial passage through the Strait for 60 days; its interpretation and implementation became contested.

facts.label: International legal and humanitarian con
facts.value: United Nations Security Council documentation has emphasized that transit passage through the Strait should not be impeded, called for protection of civilian infrastructure and commercial shipping, and urged de-escalation and diplomacy.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers a short period of escalation and negotiation in late July 2026, especially threats, maritime-security incidents and U.S. domestic war-powers debate; it does not cover the conflict's full military, diplomatic, humanitarian or regional history.
